text:
Ever seen your own boat from straight above? Off Madeira's coast, a small white speck on a lot of very blue water, and somebody up there is flying the camera so you don't have to. Our guests get that shot when the wind lets the drone fly, plus a 360 video and proper camera photos. Their hands stay free for the snacks.

What would you rather do with free hands: wave at the drone or hold a snack?
Funchal boat trips have a strange side effect: the only photo of you on holiday is taken from a drone, and you look very small. Very relaxed, though.

Two tiny yellow dots are sitting in the water below Cabo Girão, a few minutes' sail from Funchal. See if you can spot them. Small and round, side by side, a bit like eyes. Everything behind them is a pebble beach, a few terraces and a very tall cliff that doesn't fit in the photo.

If you had to guess, what are the dots? A) buoys B) the cliff's eyes
Spent a while framing this stretch of Madeira coast from the boat. The cliff is enormous, the sea is huge, and the two tiny yellow buoys in the middle are what people ask about.

The best seat on the boat is a patch of grey deck the size of a doormat, right at the front. Out of Funchal, it has two rails, a bit of anchor and nothing else between you and the water. Look past the bow and the coast is all green terraces with little white houses stacked up them like shelves. Whoever sits there gets the first look at all of it.

If you could claim one spot on a boat, would it be the very front or somewhere with a snack within reach?
Madeira from the water is mostly staircase. Every terrace has a house on it, every house has a view, and somehow nobody is out of breath down here.

Off the south coast of Madeira, the cliff does the decorating and the crew just brings a small wooden table. Red towel, pink stripy towel, a bowl of crisps, glasses raised toward the camera. Up on the cliff there's even a road with a bridge, and the cars on it only get the view for a second.

What's the one snack you'd always put on a boat table?
There's a road and a bridge near the top of this Madeira cliff. Nobody driving across gets to see the striped bit. We got the crisps, the table, and the whole wall.

A few minutes of sailing west from Funchal, the cliff starts looking like a giant tried to paint it and gave up halfway. Rust, mustard and a bit of green, all running downhill in streaks. Then, right at the bottom, a long pink wall and a pebble beach that looks very small. Only from the water do you notice how little room there is down there.

What would you name this cliff?
Madeira cliff, with a pink wall and a pebble beach squeezed in at the bottom. The cliff is the main character. The beach looks like it's only there to give the cliff a floor.

Two skippers, one steering wheel, and a small parasail floating in the sky behind us. Out of Funchal, that is the whole crew, with a hand each on the wheel and a very serious look for the camera. Our private trips carry five guests at most, and nobody else is on board.

You're on the boat and both skippers are at the wheel. Who do you hand your camera to?
Funchal skipper update: two of us, one steering wheel, and a hand each on it. Whoever is actually steering is still an open question.

Off the coast of Madeira, one guest is bent over at the very front of the boat, one hand on the rail, bare toes on the last bit of deck. Behind them, a woman with wet hair is already out of the water and watching with a small smile. The sea ahead is wide and a bit moody, and the cliff is just waiting. This is the swim stop on our Day Trip, when the sea allows. The bow does the rest.

If you were standing on that deck, would you jump first, or be the one who watches?
Swim stop off Madeira's south coast: one person crouched on the bow rail, one person watching from the side, and the sea very much not rushing anyone. Ten seconds later it's a different photo.

Funchal is slowly shrinking behind us, and the only things standing on the back rail are two white glasses that haven't been used yet. They look like proper glass, but they're plastic, because a wake like that would show real glass no mercy. The bottle is in its bucket, waiting for its turn.

So here's a small question: which of the two glasses would you say is yours, the left or the right?
Leaving Funchal with two glasses standing upright on a moving boat. They're plastic, so the wake gets no say in it. Funchal is already the size of a postcard.
